Mapping the role of industry 4.0 technologies 
in green supply chain management: 
a bibliometric and structured text analysis
Khouloud Challouf1, Abdelkarim Alhloul1* and Nikoletta Nemeth1
Discover Sustainability
Abstract
The Fourth Industrial Revolution, or Industry 4.0 (I4.0), is transforming industrial 
passages globally through the leverage of digital technologies, such as artificial 
intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), big data analytics (BDA), blockchain, and the 
Internet of Things (IoT). I4.0 has increased global competition and heightened the 
demand for sustainable supply chain solutions. Green Supply Chain Management 
(GSCM) has taken on a strategic imperative, evolving from a mere aspect of corporate 
social responsibility to assume the role of a key enabler of environmental, as well 
as economic, resilience. This present study seeks to close an important research 
gap: the lack of in-depth reviews that link various Industry 4.0 technologies with 
environmental sustainability implications in the realm of supply chain management. 
A two-phased methodological procedure was followed, integrating bibliometric 
analysis and structured text analysis. Out of 1962 peer-reviewed documents 
downloaded from Scopus and Web of Science, 49 highly cited papers were chosen 
for detailed qualitative analysis. VOSviewer and Biblioshiny were among the tools 
used to map keyword co-occurrence, co-citation networks, and thematic clusters. The 
findings show that digital technologies such as IoT, digital twins, blockchain, AI, and 
cloud computing are key enablers for waste reduction, emissions control, traceability, 
reverse logistics, and circular economy (CE) activities. The study identifies the key 
implementation challenges such as integration complexity, lack of digital skills, and 
high costs. This research stands as the first study to combine structured text analysis 
with bibliometric mapping through Scopus and WoS databases for a systematic 
investigation of Industry 4.0 technologies in Green Supply Chain Management. The 
research establishes an original analytical framework that links digital innovation to 
sustainable supply chain performance, helping academic researchers and industry 
professionals.

1  Introduction
Achieving global sustainability has become one of the most urgent priorities in the face 
of accelerating climate change, resource depletion, and growing environmental regula­
tions. The pressure to reduce carbon emissions, eliminate waste, and adopt CE models is 
forcing industries worldwide to rethink their operations. Supply chains, which account 
for a significant share of global emissions and resource use, are now central toward this 
transition. Companies are increasingly expected to adopt green practices not only to 
meet regulatory and social expectations, but also to ensure long-term operational resil­
ience and competitiveness. In parallel with these sustainability demands, a new wave 
of digital transformation, known as I4.0. The concept of I4.0 (Industrie 4.0 in German) 
emerged from a high-tech strategic initiative launched in Germany in 2011, is reshaping 
how industries operate [1, 2]. Technologies such as (AI), (IoT), (BDA), blockchain, cloud 
computing, and digital twins (DT) offer powerful tools for optimizing supply chain 
performance while also enabling environmental gains. These technologies are being 
adopted to improve traceability, enhance energy efficiency, reduce emissions, and sup­
port real-time monitoring of sustainability metrics. The integration of I4.0 with (GSCM) 
practices offers a strategic pathway toward building digitally advanced and environmen­
tally responsible supply chains. For instance, IoT sensors allow continuous monitoring 
of energy use and emissions; AI models optimize logistics and reduce fuel consumption; 
blockchain systems enhance transparency and ethical sourcing; and digital twins simu­
late environmental scenarios to guide better decision-making [3–5]. Despite the increas­
ing attention to the convergence of digital technologies and environmental concerns, 
much of the current literature remains fragmented, with limited efforts to integrate find­
ings across disciplines, sectors, and sustainability dimensions. Many studies examine 
individual technology or a specific sustainability outcome, such as emissions or waste 
[6]. Other studies gave a comprehensive overview over how evolution of sustainable 
manufacturing practices in the age of digitalization [9]. Furthermore, there is limited 
research that combines bibliometric techniques with qualitative or thematic analysis to 
map the intellectual landscape and synthesize insights from the most impactful studies 
in terms of sustainability in supply chain management, not just manufacturing [7, 8]. To 
address these gaps, the present study conducts a dual-method synthesis combining bib­
liometric mapping and structured text analysis approach was adopted, in which author 
quotes were systematically extracted and categorized according to predefined research 
questions can be seen below Table 1. To elevate the synthesis from empirical aggrega­
tion to robust theoretical interpretation, findings are anchored within three dominant

The study is guided by the following research questions:

The study examines peer-reviewed publications from the Scopus and WoS databases 
in 1962, narrowing the analysis to 49 highly cited articles. The findings reveal that IoT, 
AI, blockchain, digital twins, and cloud computing are the most frequently cited and 
impactful technologies in supporting sustainability outcomes such as waste reduction, 
emissions control, traceability, and reverse logistics. The study also identifies three com­
mon barriers to implementation cost, integration complexity, and digital skill gaps and 
proposes an analytical framework to link digital innovation with environmental perfor­
mance. This paper offers practical and theoretical contributions that will help research­
ers and decision-makers navigate the digital sustainability transition in supply chains. 
This study aims to support the advancement of sustainability goals by exploring the role 
of I4.0 technologies in green supply chain management.
2  Materials and methods
2.1  Research process
Sustainability goals in our rapidly changing economy can’t be achieved without the 
advancement of technologies in all sectors, relating I4.0 technologies to GSCM in a 
way to promote sustainability, is the aim of this study; to reach this aim a step-by-step 
process must be followed. These steps is a hybrid methodology combining bibliometric 
analysis, and structured text analysis. Process explained in detail below.
1.	 The first step in the research process is to set the keywords of the study. The keywords 
of this study have been chosen by the authors after reviewing literature, surfing all the 
related academic search engines related to the topic areas (Scopus, WoS, Emerald, 
google scholar, and ProQuest), using ML text mining techniques to choose the 
keywords.

without excluding other important documents, as pointed by expert researchers 
in the field. The key words were used in the advanced search bars in both primary

3  Results
3.1  Bibliometric analysis results (RQ1)
This section addresses RQ1 by identifying the most influential academic contributions 
at the intersection of (I4.0), (SCM), and sustainability. A comprehensive bibliometric 
analysis was conducted. From this search, 1544 documents were retrieved from Scopus 
and 409 from WoS. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, the datasets were 
refined for bibliometric mapping. Analyses were carried out using VOSviewer (v1.6.18) 
and Biblioshiny (R) to explore citation networks, keyword co-occurrence, co-authorship, 
and bibliographic coupling. The most data-intensive results are presented in Appendix A 
(Tables A1 and A2) for clarity and shortness.
3.1.1  Scopus bibliometric analysis
The initial Scopus dataset (n = 1544) was narrowed to 1493 records after applying Inclu­
sion criteria 2. This included 800 journal articles, 274 conference papers, 173 review 
articles, 165 book chapters, 37 books, and 44 conference reviews. After the final screen­
ing, Table A1 was compiled to showcase the top-cited articles check Appendix A, along 
with indicators such as Total Link Strength (TLS), journal name, and impact factor. TLS 
measures the cumulative strength of a document’s bibliographic connections within the 
dataset. The top-cited documents reveal clear thematic dominance in blockchain, big 
data analytics, and simulation-based approaches to sustainability. Noteworthy exam­
ples include: “Blockchain technology and the sustainable supply chain: Theoretically 
exploring adoption barriers” (876 citations, TLS = 128), “BDA as an operational excel­
lence approach to enhance sustainable supply chain performance” (494 citations), and 
“Digital twin for sustainable manufacturing supply chains” (207 citations). These highly 
cited works are mostly published in Journal of Cleaner Production and Resources, Con­
servation and Recycling signal an academic emphasis on resilience, traceability, and CE 
within GSCM [17]. To uncover intellectual structures, the selected articles were ana­
lyzed in VOSviewer to generate citation and bibliographic coupling maps.

even if they do not directly cite one another. Clusters emerge around technologies such 
as blockchain, simulation, and digital manufacturing, showing how parallel research

3.1.2  WoS bibliometric analysis
In parallel, the WoS search initially yielded 2021 documents, which were refined to 409 
after filtering for date range (2021–2025) and other eligibility criteria. These publications 
came from 525 sources, authored by 2916 individuals. Applying the inclusion criteria 
technique (Citation–Impact–Item), the dataset was further narrowed to 277 documents, 
of which 222 were identified as co-connected in bibliometric terms. As with Scopus, 
WoS results confirm the dominance of IoT, blockchain, BDA, and AI in sustainable SCM 
discussions. The most cited article (509 citations) focuses on IoT-enabled SCM, rein­
forcing the importance of real-time connectivity and sensor-driven monitoring in sus­
tainability transitions (Fig. 3).
Research activity is concentrated in China and India, followed by the United States, 
England, and France. This pattern highlights active scholarly engagement in both emerg­
ing economies and developed nations. Interestingly, Malaysia, Pakistan, and Iran also 
show strong contributions suggesting increasing attention to I4.0 sustainability from the 
Global South. Meanwhile, countries like Germany and the USA are less represented in 
this thematic overlap, possibly due to keyword differences or more niche research foci 
(Fig. 4).
As in Scopus, the keyword “supply chain management” dominates, affirming its cen­
trality. Other frequently co-occurring terms include “framework,” “performance,” “inte­
gration,” “innovation,” and “impact.” These keywords reflect a literature that balances 
technical advancement with strategic sustainability objectives. The recurrence of digital 
transformation terms such as “big data,” “I4.0,” “AI,” and “logistics” confirms the field’s 
focus on operational optimization, while terms like “sustainability,” “CE,” and “traceabil­
ity” reinforce the environmental lens. The consistency of keyword trends between Sco­
pus and WoS validates the thematic reliability and relevance of the research dataset.

3.2  Theoretical framework (thematic analysis results) (RQ2) What are the leading I4.0 
technologies applied in supply chain management?
3.2.1  Overview of text analysis findings
The adoption of I4.0 technologies has expanded into all aspects of daily life, starting 
from personal use to industrial applications. The technology of Radio Frequency Iden­
tification (RFID) serves multiple purposes, including identification cards, access control 
systems, and vehicle tracking. Smartphones now serve as fundamental digital interfaces 
that support secure transactions through payment systems like Apple Pay and Samsung 
Pay. The fundamental elements of I4.0 connectivity, real-time data exchange, and auto­
mation are evident in these developments. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated how 
these technologies enabled business operations through remote work, e-learning plat­
forms, and automated manufacturing lines, reducing human contact while sustaining 
production processes. Blockchain technology has enhanced supply chain visibility and 
product tracking capabilities, demonstrating how digital transformation fosters a more 
sustainable and resilient supply chain management system [18]. SCM the coordinated 
planning, execution, and monitoring of goods, information, and financial flows from ori­
gin to consumption provides a natural platform for integrating I4.0 tools and CE princi­
ples [19]. A comprehensive review of the literature, beginning with the Scopus and WoS 
databases, reveals consistent attention to various I4.0 technologies within SCM frame­
works. While there is broad agreement on a core set of technologies some divergence 
remains e.g., blockchain is excluded from some definitions of I4.0 despite its central role 
in decentralized supply chains. This study, therefore, includes blockchain as a key I4.0 
technology. Likewise, the Digital Twin, although sometimes grouped under simulation, 
is treated in this study as an independent I4.0 application due to its ability to synchronize 
digital and physical systems in real time. In addition, this research addresses the emerg­
ing I5.0 paradigm, which emphasizes human–machine collaboration, sustainability, and 
personalization. To support this analysis, Table 2 summarizes the key I4.0 technologies,

The aim of this study is to produce a comprehensive map to guide decision-makers on 
how (I4.0) technologies enable (GSCM). This is achieved through a structured text anal­
ysis review based on more than 40 documents sourced from Web of Science, Scopus, 
and other academic databases. The study addresses key research questions outlined in 
the introduction, covering the period from 2020 to 2025, while also incorporating ear­
lier literature to enhance both the depth and accuracy of the findings. These insights 
are intended to inform decision-making processes within governmental and non-gov­
ernmental organizations involved in supply chain management (SCM). The adoption 
of green practices in SCM is not solely the responsibility of firms it extends to society 
at large. This study emphasizes a fundamental principle: global supply chains are ulti­
mately shaped by human needs, which are increasingly reflected in evolving consumer 
behaviors. While SCM traditionally encompasses all stages from raw material sourcing 
to end-user delivery, the demand side, particularly consumer choice, has emerged as the 
primary driver of supply chain transformation. In today’s digital economy, a single click 
can activate complex global logistics networks. Events such as the COVID-19 pandemic 
have further accelerated these changes, with contactless delivery evolving from a public 
health strategy into a normalized and now expected consumer behavior. In this context, 
consumer responsibility becomes a critical lever for driving sustainable transformation. 
Although frameworks like consumer behavior engineering provide structured insights 
into purchasing patterns, they must now be accompanied by broader efforts to promote 
consumer awareness and accountability. Sustainable lifestyles and responsible consump­
tion habits are no longer peripheral they are central to preserving planetary health. 
However, a critical paradox emerges: the same I4.0 technologies that support greener, 
more intelligent supply chains such as (AI), (IoT), and quantum computing are them­
selves dependent on resource-intensive infrastructures. For instance, digital systems rely 
heavily on semiconductors, often referred to as the “oil” of the digital age. Additionally,

renewable energy sources are gaining traction, emerging solutions like fusion energy 
and green hydrogen are not yet mature enough to fully meet the requirements of these 
energy-intensive systems. As a result, seemingly simple digital interactions such as using 
an AI assistant carry an often-unseen but significant environmental cost. This paradox 
underscores the urgent need to balance technological advancement with ecological con­
straints. Innovation must not come at the expense of sustainability. Therefore, this study

5.4  Limitations of the study
While this study offers a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous analysis of I4.0 
and (GSCM), several limitations should be acknowledged.
First, the bibliometric analysis was limited to two major databases Scopus and WoS 
which, while extensive, may not capture all relevant literature, particularly grey litera­
ture, policy reports, and non-English publications.
This may lead to a degree of publication and language bias, especially in emerging 
regions where I4.0 and sustainability initiatives may be reported outside mainstream 
academic outlets.
Second, the inclusion criteria for selecting top-cited articles relied on quantitative 
citation metrics, such as total link strength and citation count. While these indicators 
help identify influential contributions, they may overlook newer, high-quality papers 
that have not yet accumulated significant citations but offer critical insights into nascent 
trends or regional applications for example [9] have low citation but it important in the 
research theme.
Third, although the study integrates thematic synthesis with structured text analysis 
from 40 peer-reviewed articles manly, it does not include primary empirical data col­
lection. As such, the findings are based on secondary evidence and are limited to what 
is reported in the analyzed publications. Real-time case studies, fieldwork, or expert 
interviews could further enrich and validate the observed themes, especially concerning 
sector-specific barriers and implementation contexts.
Fourth, the study focuses on I4.0 technologies but only conceptually introduces Indus­
try 5.0, without conducting a full comparative analysis of I4.0 and I5.0 paradigms.
While the connection between them is acknowledged particularly regarding human-

6  Conclusions
In conclusion, although this research offers a useful integrative framework for under­
standing how I4.0 contributes to sustainability, subsequent research is needed to dis­
till theoretical insights, remedy contextual limitations, and test practical applications 
through real-time industry experimentation. This research undertook a dual-method 
review involving bibliometric analysis and structured content synthesis to investigate 
how I4.0 technologies facilitate green practices in supply chain management (SCM). 
Based on 49 highly cited academic papers, the study determined IoT, blockchain, big 
data analytics, digital twins, and AI as principal enablers of sustainability outcomes 
across a range of supply chain functions. The results demonstrate how these technolo­
gies improve traceability, facilitate circularity, minimize emissions, and enable real-time 
monitoring and intelligent decision-making. The research further illuminates emerging 
trends associated with I5.0, including human-centric AI and collaborative robots, point­
ing to a wider transition toward socially and environmentally accountable supply chain 
paradigms. An innovative aspect of this research is the fusion of bibliometric mapping 
with thematic analysis to reveal both the intellectual structure and practical directions 
of I4.0 in sustainable SCM. The research is nonetheless limited by its confinement to 
English-language peer-reviewed articles and use of two academic databases. Follow-on 
research could therefore expand by incorporating grey literature, empirical verification, 
and cross-sectoral case studies to enhance contextual insight. This research has practical 
implications for firms and policymakers concerned with implementing digital sustain­
ability initiatives. The study exhorts firms to synchronize digital maturity with environ­
mental ambition and invest in integrated, scalable technologies. The research also makes 
a theoretical contribution to the concept of digital sustainability by charting how I4.0 
tools interact with technical, operational, and strategic strata. In line with the aims of 
Discover Sustainability, this study highlights the huge contribution of digital innovation 
in enhancing sustainable supply chain systems.

Abstract: The Fourth Industrial Revolution, or Industry 4.0 (I4.0), is transforming industrial passages globally through the leverage of digital technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), big data analytics (BDA), blockchain, and the Internet of Things (IoT). I4.0 has increased global competition and heightened the demand for sustainable supply chain solutions. Green Supply Chain Management (GSCM) has taken on a strategic imperative, evolving from a mere aspect of corporate social responsibility to assume the role of a key enabler of environmental, as well as economic, resilience. This present study seeks to close an important research gap: the lack of in-depth reviews that link various Industry 4.0 technologies with environmental sustainability implications in the realm of supply chain management. A two-phased methodological procedure was followed, integrating bibliometric analysis and structured text analysis. Out of 1962 peer-reviewed documents downloaded from Scopus and Web of Science, 49 highly cited papers were chosen for detailed qualitative analysis. VOSviewer and Biblioshiny were among the tools used to map keyword co-occurrence, co-citation networks, and thematic clusters. The findings show that digital technologies such as IoT, digital twins, blockchain, AI, and cloud computing are key enablers for waste reduction, emissions control, traceability, reverse logistics, and circular economy (CE) activities. The study identifies the key implementation challenges such as integration complexity, lack of digital skills, and high costs. This research stands as the first study to combine structured text analysis with bibliometric mapping through Scopus and WoS databases for a systematic investigation of Industry 4.0 technologies in Green Supply Chain Management. The research establishes an original analytical framework that links digital innovation to sustainable supply chain performance, helping academic researchers and industry professionals.
